title: Daily barrages of intense storms threaten flooding, damage in the Northeast … again | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

Another stormy stretch is underway in the Northeast, renewing flooding and storm damage concerns for a region that’s enduredseveral boutsin recent weeks.

Repetitive rounds of rain and storms with little reprieve between them each day began on Sunday and will continue through at least Thursday.

⛈️ Get your local forecastin the CNN Weather app☔️

Aheat domeis partially responsible: It’ssteering the jet stream— the river of air storms flow through — into the region as it bakes areas farther south with record-challenging heat.

Tuesday evening brought damaging wind gusts up to 70 mph across southeastern Pennsylvania into northern Delaware and southern New Jersey. More than 85,000 customers were without power late Tuesday, according toPoweroutage.us, as winds toppled trees and power lines across the region.

More severe thunderstorms are expected Wednesday and Thursday that could deliver damaging wind gusts, hail and even a few tornadoes.

Any storm, severe or not, could also deliver heavy rain. Flooding issues should be isolated, but any area caught under multiple storms is at the greatest risk for street flooding or rises on smaller waterways.

The forecast is basically a rinse and repeat of Tuesday’s, but the afternoon severe thunderstorm threat is shaping up to be a bit more concerning.

Strong to severe thunderstorms are possible in the morning, especially near the eastern Great Lakes. These early storms will eventually diminish and give the atmosphere enough time to recharge for another round starting in the afternoon.

Storms may still be scattered, but there could also be a fewsupercell thunderstorms. Supercells are more likely to bring stronger winds, drop larger hail and produce longer-lived tornadoes than other types of storms.

Some non-supercell storms could also congeal into  more organized lines of storms that would increase the threat of wind damage.

Wednesday’s flood threat is also higher than Tuesday’s because the storms could be stronger and move over the same areas rained on in previous days.

Rain and storm threats will start to shift away from the Northeast on Thursday, but isolated flooding issues are still possible in much of southern New England and parts of eastern New York — including New York City — New Jersey and Pennsylvania.

Stronger storms with damaging winds and hail will focus mainly on the Mid-Atlantic, including Washington, DC. Parts of southern Pennsylvania and southern New Jersey could still get clipped by these storms.

The best chance for these damaging storms is from later in the afternoon into Thursday night.

The Northeast will mostly dry out on Friday and remain that way through the weekend.
